utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours, this is case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Good afternoon to everyone. Ms. Loukas, I'm a bit surprised because we saw Mr. Stewart yesterday during the first portion of the examination-in-chief of Mr. Trbojevic and since you usually do not change when the same witness is still on ...

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, indeed, Your Honour, and it was something of a surprise to me as well but Mr. Stewart needed additional time to prepare for the cross-examination of Mr. Trbojevic, and so I had to suspend my work out of court in relation to experts and come to court today so that we could, as usual, be as ruthless as possible with balancing the priorities with in-court and out-of-court work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I might also indicate that I noticed from the transcript yesterday that Your Honours had some queries --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: -- in relation to an outstanding Defence response.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And I might indicate that response in relation to 031 et al., that response should be filed either sometime today or tomorrow. So that work is underway as we speak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think the deadline was already somewhere last week but if you say it will be filed today or tomorrow, that's accepted.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The other aspect is, I think Your Honour had another query in relation to 92 bis, if I read the transcript correctly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The other query I had, whether we could expect any response by the Defence on the additional information provided by the Prosecution on the issue of protective measures of 92 bis witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, now, Your Honour, I've been asked to clarify this. Is Your Honour referring to the confidential annex that was associated with that motion from the Prosecution to which we responded on the 24th of February or is this other additional Prosecution motion?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, the motion you're referring to is the one we had in mind, but there was an additional filing to that motion.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, out of court, we've been looking for that additional filing. I'm just wondering if perhaps the Prosecution could favour us with an additional copy and I will be able to respond to Your Honour's query as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and otherwise even the Chamber would assist you, Ms. Loukas.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I said, and even the Chamber would assist you.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: That would be wonderful, Your Honour, thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So we'll hear from that. Then finally, Mr. Stewart yesterday asked for more time to get the position of the Defence in relation to the further cross-examination of Mr. Bjelobrk.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, I noted that on the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That will not be granted. It is -- the Chamber is not very much inclined to recall Mr. Bjelobrk. Of course, unless questions to Mr. Bjelobrk are vital for the assessment of his credibility and are really necessary for the Trial Chamber for the determination of any central issue in this case. Therefore, if you make no further submissions on the importance of the matters to be raised during further cross-examination the Chamber will not of course take that into account and the Chamber will wait until the first break on Friday morning but not any longer.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I might indicate, as that is a matter that Mr. Stewart is directly involved in, I think it's prepared that I raise the matters with Mr. Stewart that Your Honour has just raised and I take it that means Your Honours have not taken a final decision in this -- in relation to this question but that you're awaiting further submissions from Mr. Stewart. Am I incorrect in that ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, that's not the correct -- at the end of the examination of Mr. Bjelobrk, there were a few matters outstanding and we went through most of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And looked at whether we could find a solution in terms of formulation of a statement and finally, we did not -- we did not come to that solution at that very moment. The parties were invited to further discuss the matters to see whether a solution could be found. The parties, as far as I understood, could agree on many points, but not on all of them. Then the Defence was invited to explain to the Chamber what the important matters were or at least what the matters were that were unresolved at that moment and I think we granted the delay now two times for that response. Now, it's the other way around. The Chamber on the basis of the material it has available will decide and cannot take anything into consideration, cannot take into account the importance of some matters as perceived by the Defence unless it is made aware of it. So therefore, if the Chamber will just proceed and will not take a decision before Friday at the end of the first -- at the end of the first morning session.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Until the first break.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Until the first break. I appreciate that. So therefore, Mr. Stewart has the opportunity to provide additional submissions between now and then, is basically the position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, if he wants to do it, he should do it by then because otherwise it might be too late.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, thank you for that clarification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If that is clear, then Mr. Tieger, are you ready to further cross-examine -- to continue the examination of your witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then Madam Usher, could you please escort Mr. Trbojevic into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Trbojevic. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Trbojevic, I'd like to remind you that you are still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony and I would also remind you if in answering any question you would fear that you would incriminate yourself that you may address the Court and we'll then rule on that whether you have to answer that question or whether you will not be compelled to do so. If you are compelled to answer a question under those circumstances, it -- the answer could not be used against you. This is just, again, for your information and I think there is no need to emphasise that the Chamber has made even one official warning during your testimony. The Chamber hopes that there is no need to repeat that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, please proceed. Examined by Mr. Tieger: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Trbojevic, let's begin with the document this afternoon found at tab 100?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Always give the number of the binder, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour; that would be binder 3.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Trbojevic, while that document is being located, I'll mention that this is a report that you had an opportunity to see yesterday when you were looking at reports to determine whether or not one of them was the Avlijas report that you recalled seeing at some time and finding ... And if I recall correctly, having looked at this report, you indicated to us that it was not the report that you had been previously referring to.

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us when you first saw this report?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're asking me now about this report before me or about the one that I was referring to as not the one that I hold now?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm referring to the report in -- before you but if I -- I don't know that you have the entire report before you at the moment, if you're just looking at that single page. What I'm referring to in terms of tab 100 is the following, sir, a cover letter from Minister Momcilo Mandic to the president of the Presidency, to the president of Republika Srpska, to president of the Assembly, and to the Prime Minister of Republika Srpska that indicates "attached herewith, please find a report," and a report to the Minister of Justice in administration?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Just to indicate, I don't know if others in the courtroom are in the same position that I am, but behind tab 100 all I find is the covering letter; there is no report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I think yesterday it was distributed in addition to what you find at this moment. So therefore -- but if you need it, we perhaps --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: In fact I do, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar has a copy -- oh, I see -- the Prosecution -- now you get the help from all sides.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: That's fantastic, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was that for Ms. Loukas or for the witness? Madam Registrar, if you provide the B/C/S -- has the witness the B/C/S copy and has Mr. Krajisnik a B/C/S copy.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: There's no problem, apparently, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Trbojevic, I'm going to give you a moment to look at that document that was just placed in front of you. I take it you had the cover letter before but not the report.

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I've looked at this one yesterday.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Correct, I think that's what I was trying to indicate in my preparatory remarks before the document was placed in front of you. And my question was: Can you tell us when you first saw this report?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't tell you that. I don't recall seeing it. I see that the date is October 1992 and I don't know if I saw it; although it is addressed to the Prime Minister so I can't exclude the possibility that it might have passed through my hands.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, if you can retain a copy of that and if you can turn your attention next, before we discuss any of the contents of the report, to tab 46 in binder 1, the 57th session of the government held on October 27th, 1992. Mr. Trbojevic, the minutes reflect that this meeting was chaired by Mr. -- by Dr. Djeric and that you were present at that meeting along with a list of attendees indicated in the first paragraph. If I could direct your attention, please, to agenda item 22.

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Agenda item 22 reflects that Momcilo Mandic, the Minister of Judiciary and Administration has informed the government on the situation in Republika Srpska camps and Assembly centres the item continues, "It is concluded that the existing illegal camps and assembly centres are to be dissolved as soon as possible. The existing penal institutions legally formed in large centres in Republika Srpska are to be used since the conditions there are suitable for legal treatment of prisoners and inmates." Now, looking at the description of Mr. Mandic's description of the topic at hand, that is the situation in the Republika Srpska camps and assembly centres and the language used in his cover letter in the title of the report, can we agree that the report found at tab 100 is the basis for Mr. Mandic's report to the 57th session of the government?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think that this follows from the document here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And having seen the minutes of the session and the agenda item, does that refresh your memory about when you first saw this report?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could only have been between the 22nd of October and the 17th of November.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There may be -- I'm looking at a few dates on the document, sir, that -- the document itself and the submission date by Mr. Mandic on the cover letter is 22 October 1992, you date you mention in your response, and the government session was held on 27th of October, 1992, although it appears -- the minutes appear to have been transcribed on the 17th of November. So were you indicating that you could only have seen this document between the 22nd of October and the 27th of October?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. And the 27th of October.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The conclusion reached by the government was the existing illegal camps and assembly centres were to be dissolved as soon as possible. Can you tell us which existing illegal camps and assembly centres Mr. Mandic was referring to, or that the government was referring to in its conclusion that they should be dissolved?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One could probably read it from this report, this information that he provided. Legal venues of detention at the time could only have been prisons, district prisons. Such existed in Doboj, Banja Luka. I can't speak now from memory, but none of the titles mentioned here or rather towns, Vlasenica, Zvornik, Brcko, Prijedor, Sanski Most, Teslic, Ilidza, Hadzici, none of these could have been legal. As far as I know, there isn't a single decision on the establishment of any centres there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there a discussion by the government about the report or any aspects of the prisons or collection centres before the conclusion that was reached in the agenda item we've looked at?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume that we must have had some discussion about it but who the participants to this discussion were and how the discussion, if any, was conducted, I can't say. The minutes don't reflect that sort of thing. The minutes do not say that a discussion was held and that the following persons participated in it, it merely says that a conclusion was adopted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Trbojevic, Judge Hanoteau has one or more questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, actually, I have a question I would like you to clarify something. Yesterday, I understood that somehow, you were blaming the Minister of Justice or the Minister of Home Affairs not to present reports to the government but you were saying that these two ministers had regretfully, if I remember rightly your opinion, had regretfully the tenancy to directly report to Mr. Krajisnik and Karadzic. This is quite in contradiction with the documents which are submitted to us today because this case, the Minister of Justice makes a presentation to the government on a report. Is there not a contradiction in all this? I'm just -- I would like you to clarify things.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This report which is before us right now is addressed to the Prime Minister, among others. It was on the agenda, it was an agenda item at the government session and I have no doubts that it was indeed delivered to the Prime Minister. However, in the previous months, there were various instances of communication between -- there were various instances in which the communication between the Minister of Justice, Minister of the Interior and the Prime Minister was disrupted, practically.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] According to you, this means the Minister of Justice, the Minister of Home Affairs no longer were attending government meetings, government sessions; is that what you actually mean to say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't say that they never attended government sessions but I could say that on a number, significant number of occasions, they were absent from sessions and I think that that is reflected in the minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have one additional question as well. You say you do not remember exactly who spoke during this 27th of October government session on the report. Was part of the discussion whether or not it should be investigated and, if need be, prosecutions should be instituted against those who had created or maintained those illegal detention facilities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that that was not discussed, otherwise it would have been recorded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So finally, when you got the information, no action apart from at least the intention that was expressed to dismantle these camps was taken; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One of the reasons we looked at the report yesterday was that it was prepared by Mr. Avlijas and submitted by Mr. Avlijas as it indicates in the last page of the text of the document before the lists that are appended. Let me ask you a couple of questions first about the contents of the document. Mr. Avlijas indicates, "Inspections and conversations with responsible organs in the following places," the first page he refers to Vlasenica. And in Vlasenica he states that he toured the location with the commander of the police, the Vlasenica police station, Mr. Stanic, and was told by Mr. Stanic that "at the beginning of combat activities, a number of people of Muslim nationality were isolated in that place or were exchanged for people of Serbian nationality." If you turn to the passage in Zvornik, in the second paragraph, Mr. Avlijas refers to 64 people of -- he refers in the first paragraph to 64 people of Muslim nationality, and in the second paragraph points out the problem of what to could with the detainees because "the other side is refusing to conduct an exchange." Can you explain to me, Mr. Trbojevic, why the reluctance or refusal by the other side to conduct an exchange has an impact on the continued detention of these 64 people?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see how I would be in a position to know that. I didn't know, at the time, that they had 64 detainees. I also did not offer them for exchange and consequently, I cannot know why the other side did not take them in through the exchange.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did any member of the government, having been presented with this report, inquire as to whether or not -- inquire about why these people were being held and why their continued detention depended upon the willingness or unwillingness of the other side to conduct an exchange?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether somebody did inquire. As for this particular case, I know nothing about it. In some other cases, I know that Dr. Karadzic gathered information on the treatment of persons detained in such sites. About the process of exchange and so on as a Minister of Health.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter's correction, it wasn't Dr. Karadzic, it was Dr. Kalinic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Insofar as I can tell from this report, Mr. Trbojevic, Mr. Avlijas indicates nothing about either the condition of the people who are detained or the reason for their confinement. Weren't both those issues matters of interest for the government?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In here, it simply states that they had been arrested in the course of combat operations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I ask you the question quite directly. The report states that, "There was a problem what to do with the detainees because the other side is refusing to conduct an exchange." At the end of the report, it says that they are "kept without legal grounds for keeping them." What, in your view, should be the answer if you keep someone detained without a legal basis, if someone else is not willing to exchange them, what should you do with those illegally held?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They ought to be released --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you for that answer. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- naturally.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I note that in the last section of the report referring to Hadzici, again, it appears that Mr. Avlijas indicates that their continued a confinement or release depends upon an exchange that may or may not take place. Is that right, or did you understand that differently?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can see, based on this document, Avlijas proposed that they be transferred to Butimir which was a penitentiary institution; however, that was refused because they wanted to exchange them for the Serbs imprisoned in Turcin and in a school in Razavic -- Pazaric, at least this is what is stated here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What steps, if any, did the government, the president of the Assembly, the Presidency of Republika Srpska or any of those to whom this report was submitted take in response to that information?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I am aware, they did nothing about it; however, I cannot be fully certain of this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I note in the report, among other things, that in attempt to go verify a report by the ICRC that a large number of citizens of Muslim nationality had been liquidated, and the figure quoted was about 2.500, Mr. Avlijas met with the president of the municipality, the president of the --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Just prior to Mr. Tieger continuing, if we could just have a reference to where in the report Mr. Tieger's referring to

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I apologise. I thought I had said Brcko, which is item number 3, but I see I failed to do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In any event, said he met with the president of the municipality, the president of the Executive Board, and the deputy in the Assembly. Mr. Trbojevic, do you have any reason to doubt that the allegations by the ICRC were that people of Muslim nationality had been killed by Bosnian Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Listen, it's such a general question, what can I tell you, I have no reason to doubt the ICRC report; however, I cannot confirm it either.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the time --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Just in relation to that question --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Ms. Loukas.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: So sorry, my microphone. Thank you. Just in relation to that question from Mr. Tieger in relation to the section of the report quoted there in relation to Brcko, Mr. Tieger, in his question, interpolated killed by Bosnian Serb forces and Your Honour, that, of course, is not part of the section of the report that Mr. Tieger refers to and if there is going to be some paraphrasing of what's contained in the report, I'd ask that that there be some level of accuracy in that regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Loukas -- yes, Mr. Tieger -- no, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I gather the Court understands the point but I'll make my point, if I may. I didn't -- I wasn't paraphrasing the report. I don't think -- I think it was clear I was not going doing so. I was merely asking the witness -- I was referring his attention to the report by the ICRC and ask if it was understood that the ICRC was making allegations that the murder victims ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just -- your question was, Mr. Tieger: "Mr. Trbojevic, do you have any reason to doubt that the allegations by the ICRC were that people of Muslim nationality had been killed by Bosnian Serb forces." That is a question which could be understood in different ways. Whether there was any doubt that they were killed or that they were killed by Bosnian forces, at least the perpetrators do not appear in this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, if I can clarify and maybe this distinction wasn't clear enough, but I wasn't asking him with any reason to doubt the allegations themselves, I wasn't asking him to cast a judgement about the accuracy of those allegations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That was not sufficiently clear in your question, yes. Please proceed and perhaps you reformulate the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The question is this Mr. Trbojevic, the ICRC obviously issued a report that was of concern and Mr. Avlijas was responding to. That report alleged that a large number of Muslims had been liquidated in the town. Now, did you and the others at the time you were looking, you were reviewing the report by Mr. Avlijas understand that the ICRC wasn't looking at random crimes of Muslims but that the ICRC had alleged that Muslims were killed during the course of ethnic cleansing by Bosnian Serb forces? Was that your understanding or did you think that Mr. Avlijas was looking at allegations by the ICRC of killings that occurred for some other reason?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, just in relation to that question, it is, I would submit, rather awkwardly put and, of course, whilst I appreciate that the witness is a man who has, of course, some prior legal background, nevertheless, the way the question is posited in relation to understanding of others and two alternatives, it's very awkward, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's put it very directly to the witness. In the report it says, Mr. Trbojevic, that the Red Cross had issued an alarming report, that it said that a large number of citizens of Muslim nationality, 2.500, had been liquidated in that town. Did you understand this report to include a -- even if it was an implicit suggestion as to whom could be blamed for that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Based on what I knew, based on my information, the Serb side was the dominant one as far as the war operations were concerned; therefore, if there were any victims, it was believed that that was the consequence of war operations conducted by Serb units. This is something that, in my view, was implicitly stated in such a report. Now, as for the figure of 2.500 people, I have to say that even today, I believe that it is not probable that the figure is so high.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, any ground for that? You say you believe that, is there any -- do you have any objective data to ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do not. I was not in the vicinity of Brcko.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you have any reason why you say that you -- I do understand from your answer that the Serb side was dominant so if they were talking about 2.500 persons liquidated, whether the number was correct or not is another matter, that they were blaming, that it was suggested that the Serbs were to be blamed for that. Do you have any specific reason why you included in your answer that this was for war operations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I suppose that it had to occur in the course of war operations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What do you understand by "war operations"? Combat activities or would that include also, well, let's say destroying civilian dwellings or killing civilians, that would be included in your concept of war operations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't view an attack against civilian peaceful population as an aspect of a war operation, certainly not. I naturally did see what Brcko looked like. I saw part of the town which was demolished, destroyed, practically. However, based on the information I received from the -- from a deputy, I think his name was Dr. Bijelic, I'm not quite sure about his name but his nickname was Beli, therefore, the information he gave me was that that part of Brcko was the front line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In view of your understanding that the allegations by the ICRC were focused, at least implicitly, upon Serbs, did it concern you that Mr. Avlijas had only talked to representatives of the Serb authorities?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see how he would be able to talk with the representatives of the Muslim authorities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did that resolve the issue, as far as you were concerned, about the allegations by the ICRC?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say that I thought the matter to be resolved.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that mean that you found Mr. Avlijas's conclusions or the basis for his conclusions inadequate?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Just in relation to that, Your Honours, firstly, we're dealing with a document that the witness, in his previous evidence, clarified that he hadn't remembered seeing. Then he was taken back to the session, the government session at which he was present and asked whether or not he recalled a debate on the issue and said that he couldn't and it wasn't -- I'm paraphrasing here, but it wasn't recorded there as having taken place and he couldn't recall and what have you. I'm concerned that we're now getting into quite some realm of speculation, particularly when we're taking into account the witness's previous answers in reels to this area, and also taking into account that we're dealing with quite some precise aspects of the report from 13 years ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And if any of us in court were asked to recall the precise details of papers that we've seen, for example, in a legal case we were doing 13 years ago, there may be some trouble with that concept, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas, I do understand your concerns. At the same time, the memory of Mr. Trbojevic has been refreshed and he's not asked to speculate on matters but he is asked on how he interprets or has interpreted this report, how he reads it or may have read it.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I'm happy if the questions remain at that level, Your Honour, I'm just concerned that we're going to veer over into that speculative and grey area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Tieger, I think your question was: When reading the report now, Mr. Trbojevic, and perhaps also as you read the report when you saw it in October 1992, did you have any concern about the sources Mr. Avlijas used in order to draw his conclusions, them being one sided.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't say that I was concerned. I did not speak to Avlijas specifically on this issue. I knew that there was a commission for exchanges and that these commissions drafted lists of persons to be exchanged and corpses to be exchanged. And it was understood that the matter would be fully disclosed by way of these lists.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The question was whether the -- Mr. Avlijas reporting exclusively on conversations he had with Serbs, whether you had any concern on whether that would create a balanced picture of the situation on the ground?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is stated in the report that he had talked to representatives of Serb authorities. It is absolutely clear that he talked only to one side and since he belongs to the same side, it was assumed that he received accurate data for the report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And you also said how could he have talked with representatives of the Muslims. Why could he not have done so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To tell you the truth, I don't know. As far as I am aware, the only contacts, the only correspondence that existed was between those commissions for exchanging people. I don't know that the government of Republika Srpska talked with the Muslim government at all. I know that there was one discussion with the government of Herceg-Bosnia and I'm not aware of any other contacts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Does it also implicitly say that there were no Muslim representatives left in the territory controlled by the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Why could you not have -- you said how could he have talked with representatives of the Muslims. Why not? You just go to them and have a conversation with them, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know that any such thing took place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm asking why it was impossible. You said in your earlier answer, if you would like me to find it, I'll quote to you. It's just before Judge -- I'll find that -- if you would like me to quote it literally, I'll find it for you, but ... One second, please. If anyone could help me --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I'm also looking, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm just trying to find the line.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I think it's at the top of page 19 that Your Honour is referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger then put the following question to you, "In view of your understanding that the allegations by the ICRC were focused at least implicitly upon the Serbs, did it concern you that Mr. Avlijas had only talked to representatives of the Serb authorities?" Then your answer was, "I don't see how he would be able to talk with the representatives of the Muslim authorities." You just said that you didn't know whether it happened, but your testimony was that you did not see how that was possible. My question is: Why was that not possible?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know how to explain this to you. There was a war on. How could, in such a situation, one go to the opposite side without having a way of arranging it, such an encounter, in advance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Wasn't it true that in Brcko, at least a large part of the municipality were under Serb control.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes. As far as I know, there was one Croat municipality. I don't recall how it was called. But yes, most of the territory was held by Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Couldn't they have talked, then, to the representatives of the Muslims on that Serb-held territory?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know that they did talk to the other side, and I don't know who it could have been on the other side that they could have talked to, and I don't know whether it would have been necessary at the time for them to talk to someone who was on the Muslim-held territory. I don't know, really.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Were there any Muslims left on Serb-held territory to be represented and to be partner in a conversation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Probably there were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Why could they not have talked to them? I mean we are talking about an alarming report of 2.500 people being liquidated. Why not talk to those who belong to the ethnicity reportedly being liquidated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it would have definitely been better to talk to the side whose victims they were, but the figures about the number of those killed or otherwise perished could not have been provided by someone who could not have gone out of their houses, who were enemies to the military that was in the town. It isn't possible for an individual to provide information concerning the entire town or an area. It says here that some of the victims were buried in a savage, brutal and heinous manner and -- or rather with the special religious ceremony, and I'm not really sure how Avlijas could have come by that information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So you say it was of no use to talk to them because they could not possibly provide any useful information.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One could hardly expect to get such information from the Muslim side, merely through talking with a person or two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In Brcko.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, you talked to ten, or to their representatives. Okay. It was none of your concern at that moment and you thought this information to be a reliable basis of the report of Mr. Avlijas, is that a correct understanding, although you say that it may have been better, although it would have no real result if you would have talked to one or two Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just indicate, in relation to that there do seem to be rather a number of questions in one in the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm trying to summarise the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And if he does not agree with it, if he thinks that it's not a fair summary, he can say in what respect it is not correct. I included only matters that were --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The gist of it is the way you put it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And just a couple of questions in connection with Mr. Avlijas. Mr. Avlijas had previously been, at least for a period of time, president of the Commission for Exchange; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was on various commissions all the time, if you know what I mean. I do think, however, that he was on this commission as well. After the war, he was a member of the commission that was searching for those who had perished or went missing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To save time, I'm not going to direct your attention -- pull it out and direct your attention to it specifically, but behind tab 28, there is the appointment of Mr. Avlijas at a government session. But for purposes of this discussion, can we agree on that? But I'm more than happy to show you the document.

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not doubt that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Tieger, before we move away before these documents, I'd like to ask a question to the witness. About the way the report was submitted to the government, it was on the 17th of November, 1992. Do you have the minutes in front of you, Witness? We read that the session was chaired by Ranko Delic [as interpreted], 57th session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's said Djeric and not Delic since that is well known.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On that first page we read [In English] "a decision where Milan Trbojevic" [Interpretation] and that's you. And then we read a number of other names, Markovic, who is that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Petra Markovic was a lady, Minister of Finance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What was his position.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Bogdan Subotic was Defence minister.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there any French translation? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We didn't get the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But I didn't have my microphone on. On channel 5, we received French interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can hear you. What was the answer regarding Mr. Subotic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Bogdan Subotic was Defence minister.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And what about Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mico Stanisic was Minister of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mandic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Momcilo Mandic was Minister of Justice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Velibor Ostojic was Minister of Information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Kalinic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Dr. Dragan Kalinic, Minister of Health.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Antic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Bozidar Antic, Minister of Commerce.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Zukovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ljubomir Zukovic, Minister of Education.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then we see other names, four lines of names. Are these people ministers? Who are these people, Lakic, Peric, Nedic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Lakic was the secretary administrative secretary to the government. And the other one was the -- one of the officials in the Ministry of Health. Nedic, as for Nedic, I don't know. And I see that there's another person on behalf of Pavle Vidojevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, could we say that these are secretaries to ministers, people working with ministers? Okay, that's right. During that session, it is announced that there are illegal camps, places where people are gathered that are illegal, assembly centres. You stated that you did not remember what happened when the existence of these camps was announced; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From the minutes, one can see that the conclusion has been reached that they all had to be detained [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but during the session, do you remember the atmosphere, do you remember what was said, how people reacted when it was stated that there were illegal camps?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, if people had protested, would you remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I probably would.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You do not remember that you, yourself, protested?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are asking about protesting against something that had been established as existing. I did not protest in any way because I simply did not have anyone to express my protest to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me for insisting on that point, but you're a lawyer. You are aware of the major principles related to the protection of citizens and individuals. You are aware of the principles pertaining to arbitrary detentions and the way they are condemned and you say that you did not make any protests. Why? Why didn't you say anything? There must be a reason for that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yesterday, I tried to explain that nobody in their right mind could even start imagining what sort of camps these were. It transpires from these reports that there are detainees --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's be very specific. I'm not talking about the living conditions in the camps, I'm not interested in that at all. I'm saying the following: You hear that there are illegal detention centres. I'm asking you why you did not react when you learned that? My very is question clear.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The conclusion was adopted that these centres had to be closed down right away and there was nobody I could react in relation to because it wasn't either Mandic or Stanisic who ordered for these camps to be opened and neither did the government. Therefore, who would I express my protest to? This was at the point when we were adopting a decision to the effect that these had to be closed down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could one be completely moved and shocked when hearing the news?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We were shocked and I, myself, stated that publicly on one of the TV shows shortly afterwards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just a minor point of clarification, if I may. I think in indicating the date on which the report was submitted, Judge Hanoteau was looking at the -- what may be the transcription date of November 17th. I think the date of the session was October 27th. A minor matter. Witness, you said that, "There was nobody I could react in relation to because it wasn't either Mandic or Stanisic who ordered for these camps to be opened and neither did the government." Who did order the camps to be opened?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who had the power to order the camps to be opened?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody had that power.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Somebody clearly had that power because those camps were opened, sir. Then the -- within the?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object to that question, it's not a proper question, it's argumentative.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Within --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There seems to be some confusion about legal authority, that's the way of understanding the word "power," and the factual power someone exercises even if there's no legal ground for that. Could you please avoid that confusion in your questions to the witness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: First of all, Mr. Trbojevic, you said that Mr. Mandic and Mr. Stanisic did not order the camps opened; how do you know that and on what basis do you say that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did qualify my answer by saying "as far as I know." And I don't know that they did issue such orders.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which, if any, of the ministers who attended the session to discuss the camps were responsible for the arrest or detention or confinement of persons within the territory of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is well-known and -- that it's the police that has the authority to arrest people under such circumstances. Another well-known fact is that the army can carry out such arrests. It is also only natural that the military should have prisoners of war during wartime, during war operations, and these must have been the structures carrying out these arrests.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And following those arrests, the people arrested were placed into the camps that we've been talking about; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Today, I know that this was the case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who maintained or ran those camps?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I can't answer that. One can only presume that the municipality at hand provided food, water, and other necessary supplies. One can assume that the army might have taken upon itself the responsibility to provide part of these supplies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What efforts did the government or any other organ of the Bosnian Serb political authorities make to determine who was running and maintaining the camps?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think that question needs some focussing in terms of what time period Mr. Tieger is asking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I understand the questions to be related to the summer of 1992, not later than to the report of Mr. Avlijas in October 1992; is that a correct understanding?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, as long as that's made clear.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Beyond the reports that we discussed here, I don't know of any other activities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I put one of these questions again quite directly to you. In the summer of 1992, you described reports from the media, barbed wire, well, you know exactly what it is, you've talked about Omarska. At almost every session of the government - of course not, I'm exaggerating - but at many sessions of the government, sometimes at a moment which seems to coincide very much with media reports, the question of prisons, prison camps, exchanges are discussed again and again and again. Are you telling us that never anyone said, "Who is responsible for these camps? Who should take responsibility for these camps?" Did that never happen or was that not necessary because it was clear who had the responsibility or was it not any government minister that was responsible and that was clear? Tell us what happened at that moment. But it's difficult to believe. It's difficult to believe that this frequency of discussing the matter of people being sent to make a tour, exchange commissions, that no one ever thought, "Who is responsible for this?" Could you tell us what the feeling was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Beyond that which we have seen in these reports here, I don't know that there were any other government activities. Based on these reports, one can see that the government did not have the accurate -- an accurate picture of what was going on on the ground.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but that was not my question. My question was -- and it related not only to these reports, but also to the sessions, the creation of exchange commissions, the instructions given to report on detention facilities. No one ever asked, "Who is responsible?"

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I know, nobody did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was it that you were convinced that no one within your circle, that is the government, the ministers of the government, were responsible, that the responsibility was somewhere outside?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know how to explain this. It was not a result of an analysis carried out by us. These were simply the events that took us by surprise. Once we learned, to some extent, about what was going on, we concluded that those sites had to be shut down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And whose responsibility was that to do that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Today, as we analyse this, it is clear that it was the responsibility of all of us who were members of the government.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And at that time, was it one specific minister, was it the Prime Minister, was it none of the ministers, was it the collectivity of the government?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Prime Minister, myself, as Deputy Prime Minister for internal policy, Minister of Police, Minister of Justice, Minister of Defence and Minister of Health. Each of us had within scope of their authorities also an aspect that linked it to this issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did it then happen? Were the camps closed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I know, yes, they were closed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At what -- in what period of time, approximately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. I think that some of them had been shut down even before we adopted this conclusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How did you know that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Within the past 10 years, this matter was reported widely in the papers and various documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So you didn't know at that time, it's only later on that you learned that some of these camps were closed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely so. I think that one week after this session, or perhaps several weeks after this session, the government was dismissed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Tieger, please proceed. I look at the clock and I'm aware that quite some time has taken from you by the Bench at this moment. We will adjourn until a quarter past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, just before we proceed, there's just one matter I think that needs to be clarified. It's just on page 27 of the LiveNote transcript and it's in relation to the questions from His Honour Judge Hanoteau and it's at line 21.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Choose the one on the right or choose the one on the left.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed. Perhaps I should bring them together. It's at page 27, line 20 and 21 on that page, in response to a question from His Honour Judge Hanoteau, the witness indicated "From the minutes one can see that the conclusion has been reached that they all had to be detained." It seems to me that that may in fact be a misinterpretation because when one looks at the minutes, it doesn't actually say that so I'm just wondering whether that could be clarified before we proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think it's in my memory that it was that the witness said different, that it's --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And since he only referred to the minutes, I think it's clear that he meant that the --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Dissolved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There could hardly be any doubt on that.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Trbojevic, yesterday, during the course of discussion about the government session of 15 June, and the reasons why the working group mentioned at that session did not undertake action, you said the following, and that's found at page 11503: "At that time, there were exchange commissions within each corps. In each region, exchanges were carried out so we believed that the system was functioning." Now, first of all, Mr. Trbojevic, when you were referring to exchange commissions within each corps, were you referring to a geographic core or corps referring to in military terms?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had in mind military units when I said "within each corps." And as far as I know, exchange commissions also had their lower units and I don't know when each of them was formed; however, later on, we learned that there were various exchange commissions that were in operation and that more or less, commanders of military units arranged meetings with the opposite side and exchanged various lists and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As I mentioned the time this -- that that -- those comments were made was in the context of the discussion about the June 15th minutes and the working group that was tasked at that session and your feelings about the failure of the working group to fulfill that task. So you said and explained in part, as I mentioned, "At that time were there were exchange commissions ..." et cetera. Did you and the other members of the working group formed on June 15th know about the work of the exchange commissions within each corps that you mentioned in the course of your answer?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've explained that. I did not have in mind corps alone. I personally had no knowledge about the work of the exchange commissions. Later on, I learned some things from colleagues that had been members of such commissions. Now, as to whether the others might have had some insight into the operations of these commissions, I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I wasn't asking you for all the details about how the commissions worked, but you said yesterday that those commissions, in general, existed in each region, exchanges were carried out and you said, "So we believe the system was functioning."

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you to take a look, please, at an order found behind tab 120 in binder 4. Tab 120 is an addition that has been provided to the Registry along with a number -- or will be provided to the Registry at this point, along with a number of other additions. Mr. Trbojevic, tab 120 contains an order signed by Commander Major Svetozar Andric of the Birac Brigade dated 28 May 1992 and the order is enumerated in seven parts. If I can direct your attention to item number six which states, "The moving out of the Muslim population must be organised and coordinated with the municipalities through which the moving is carried out. Only women and children can move out while men fit for military service are to be placed in camps for exchange." Focussing on the second sentence of that enumerated item, was it consistent with your understanding of how the exchange system was to work, that women and children would be able to move out while military-age men were to be placed in camps for exchange?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said nothing of the kind, nothing even resembling that. This is a commander of a brigade who is writing to the staff. I neither know who Svetozar Andric is, nor do I know where the staff of the Zvornik Brigade was or anything about this letter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Trbojevic, could you just tell me what the question is you were answering?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The question was formulated in such a way as though I had stated that the women and children were to be exchanged whereas men fit for military service had to do something else. I said nothing of the kind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You were asked, and please listen carefully to the questions put to you, whether what you see in this letter, whether that was consistent with how you understood how the exchange system was to work.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is being implied here that I understood something that was going on. My understanding was that all prisoners had to be exchanged for all other prisoners. That was my position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So this does not -- this is not consistent with your understanding of the exchange system and I take it that the next question by Mr. Tieger would have been what, then, would have been your understanding of the exchange system. You said, "All prisoners had to be exchanged for other prisoners."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Naturally. Here I had in mind prisoners of war, not persons who had been arrested on the basis of legal grounds or convicted or sentenced.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was it your view that the exchange of prisoners were -- was strictly confined to prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I suppose that the prisoners of war are precisely the category that is created in war times and who need to be exchanged.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not asking you whether you were of the opinion that prisoners of war should be exchanged. My question was whether you -- whether it was your understanding that the exchange of prisoners was limited to prisoners of war.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Just before Mr. Tieger proceeds, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Just in relation, and at this point I'm just putting a marker down, and that is that this sort of evidence, in my submission, should be -- can be elicited and should be elicited on the basis of open questions from Mr. Tieger rather than with confusing references to documents that the witness has not seen. So in essence the questions and in fact the substance of what Mr. Tieger's questions were directed to, and as a consequence what Your Honour's questions were directed to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: -- were questions that did not need the interpolation of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I place that there as a marker.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand what you say, Ms. Loukas, it at voids at least five or ten minutes debate and disguise of questioning on whether this was anything realistic even to think about. So therefore I do not oppose that much against this way of putting the questions. It's just giving an example and asking whether that example fitted into the understanding of the witness. But in general, I would agree with you but under these specific circumstances, you only put a marker, you made no objection, I carefully notice that.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour, can the witness be shown the document behind tab 75 which is located in binder 2.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Trbojevic, the document found at tab 75 is dated June 6th, 1992. It's an order signed by the Chairman of the Commission for Exchange of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina Mr. Rajko Colovic who was mentioned earlier in evidence. The last page indicates the bodies to which the order was delivered including the government of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the Ministry of Justice, the MUP, et cetera. Does this document, Mr. Trbojevic, reflect an order related to the system of exchanges?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It seems to have been adopted by the president of the Central Commission for Exchanges.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I direct your attention to a portion of the document found on page 3 of the English translation. It appears after the single-sentence paragraph: "The implementation of this order shall be monitored by an authorised the employee of the Ministry of Justice or the president of the higher or basic court," that might orient you. And then it states all women not arrested during combat activities and whose detention is not related to combat activities, all children and minors up to the age of 16, all the elderly, infirm, and ill shall immediately be released and allowed freedom of movement in accordance with their wishes without conditions and exchanges." Have you found that paragraph, sir, and have you had an opportunity to look at it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us, if you know, what was to happen to the men over the age of 16 and who were not elderly, inform, or ill, who were not arrested during combat activities and whose detention is not related to combat activities?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not stated here. Or rather, further below, it is stated that the exchanges are to be conducted in accordance with the principle all for all on the so-called no-man's land. Therefore, based on this document, it seems that the others were to be exchanged.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you said yesterday, "So we believed that the system was functioning," is this the manner in which you believe the system to be functioning on or around June 15th, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Listen, this document here contains instructions, some central commission here is issuing instructions to be implemented in the field. It was to be expected that they would act in accordance with this document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And again, Mr. Trbojevic, I ask you, when you said, "So we believed that the system was functioning," is this the way in which you understood the system to be functioning in mid-June 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not read every word so I can't claim that this is exactly how things were unfolding; however, based on the bits that I did read, and based on what you just quoted, I assumed that and that the others were to be exchanged as soon as possible in accordance with the principle all for all. Those ought to have been the rules that applied to this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Trbojevic, yesterday, we spoke about 400 Muslims from Bratunac who were held in Pale on the 14th through the 17th of May, 1992, and then transferred to Visoko -- sorry, I believe they were transferred on the 16th of May. And I asked you about the arrival of a group of that number and you provided us some information about what would be known or not known about such a group in a location the size of Pale. Let me ask you to look next at three documents, the first of which is found at tab 122. Tab 122 contains an order which bears the typed name of Dr. Branko Djeric which is not signed dated May 15th, 1992 which states, "The Sokolac Crisis Staff is obligated to provide 3 trucks (including tarpaulins) that are to be used for the transport of prisoners from Pale to Visoko via Ilijas." Paragraph 2, "The order is effective immediately." If the witness can be provided with 123 and 124 as well. Tab 123 is also an order dated 15 May 1992. It also bears the typed name of Professor Branko Djeric above the title "President of the government," and it states at the top, according to the -- item 20, paragraph 5 of the law regarding government - I'm making the order - one, Crisis Staffs: "Sokolac has the obligation to provide three trailer trucks (with canvass cover) and put them in disposition of the Crisis Staff Pale on the 16th of May at 0800 hours. Tow trucks will be returned the same day." Number 2: "The order is effective immediately." And tab 124 contains a document dated 15 May 1992 for the Crisis Staff Ilijas, "Please approve and provide the passage through your territory for the group of prisoners who are presently at Pale and travelling to Visoko. Transport and escort for those prisoners will be provided by the Crisis Staff Pale. Please destroy that approval the moment when the prisoners leave Ilijas municipality." It bears the name of government secretary Nedjeljko Lakic [phoen], stamped and signed. Now, is this process of exchange that took place in mid-May 1992, Mr. Trbojevic, consistent with your understanding of how the exchange process was to be conducted?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, just in relation to that, those -- the documents themselves don't appear ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you would not mind, Ms. Loukas, I think I can imagine, but perhaps without explaining to the witness already at this time what the problem might be. What specific aspect we are talking about, transportation of persons. Is it that you would like to know whether it was the usual -- it was within the understanding of the witness that transport would be organized by Crisis Staffs or would it be that they start at 8.00 in the morning or whatever? Yes, could you please put your question in such a way that -- I take it, Ms. Loukas, since the Chamber received at least some evidence on the -- well, let's say on the composition of the convoy that -- which of course is not clear, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I think that Your Honour's clarification certainly meets the basis of my objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Trbojevic, was it your understanding that the exchange of prisoners would sometimes entail coordination between municipalities over which those prisoners would have to travel?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose that the municipality across the territory of which they pass should know of that. Now, I'm -- it is not up to me to say whether this was the proper way of approaching this or not because I do not know who the other party with whom this had been arranged with was, or in which way it had been arranged. Specifically speaking about this case, I didn't know anything about it because at that point in time, I was not in Pale yet.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I believe that yesterday you looked at tab 74 in connection with the exchange of these particular Muslim prisoners, and in particular you looked at page 3 of the list that was provided which indicated the signature of Mr. Markovic, a member of the government's commission on behalf of the Serbian MUP for the exchange of prisoners of war. Slobodan Markovic. Do you recall that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Based on your view of the list and, in particular, Mr. Markovic's position and signature, and based on the documents you've seen this afternoon, is there anything about the process reflected in those documents that is not consistent with your general understanding of how the exchange of prisoners was to -- how the system of exchange was to be conducted?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are asking me to talk about things that I did not take part in. The instructions set down by the president of the central commission said that conditions had to be put in place in order for prisoners to go wherever they wished to go. Others had to be exchanged in cooperation with the commission on the other side. Whether there was any agreement or approval for such exchanges, I don't know. We saw the list of people who were exchanged but there is -- I can't tell you anything more specifically than I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand that, Mr. Trbojevic, you can't tell us anything about this particular exchange that you don't know about. I'm simply asking you, in light of what you've had an opportunity to see, and in light of your explanation to us that you understood, at least in mid-June, the system to be functioning, if there's anything about what you see here which is inconsistent with or incompatible with your understanding of how the system was to function?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, just in relation to that, I think the question as posed is somewhat amorphous, particularly the reference to what you see here. If the witness is required to answer on the basis of certain documents, I think the documents should be specified so that -- in all fairness to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Trbojevic, you said that the working group on the exchange of prisoners, I think you said they never met, and there was no problem because everything seemed to be fine. What Mr. Tieger is trying to find out is what you knew about the exchange of prisoners on the basis of documents he's presenting to you. He's confronting you with a transport of 400 people travelling through different municipalities. What did you actually know, not about how things should have gone, but how they actually went? And just to inform you, this Chamber has received a considerable amount of evidence on detained peoples who certainly were not prisoners of war. This Chamber has received quite a bit of evidence on exchange of detained persons which hardly could be considered prisoners of war. So what we'd like to know and what Mr. Tieger would like to know is what did you actually know about the practice of exchange of prisoners? And if you say, "I didn't know anything about it," then please tell us. If you knew anything about it, tell us also. And Mr. Tieger is mainly interested to know whether you were aware, especially that not all men of military age that were detained were, perhaps -- that some of them might have been civilians and nevertheless be there for exchange, whether any women were under the detained people, whether they really were released or not, whether there were any minors, any children. What do you know about it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Nothing concrete, Your Honour. I was not involved in these matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Nevertheless, you concluded yesterday that there was hardly any need to pay any further attention to the exchange because everything, just to say it in simple words, went fine, without any concrete knowledge on what happened on the ground. Is that a correct understanding of your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you've understood me well. I said that according to our knowledge to what we knew about it, there was no need for us to interfere with these matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And now I do understand you had no concrete knowledge but on the basis of the absence of any concrete knowledge, you were satisfied that there was no need to do anything.
